Motion to Intervene Out of Time and Comments of Antora Energy LLC In Response to the 
Commission’s Co-location Order 
 
Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission” 
order instituting a Federal Power Act (“FPA”) section 206 proceeding concerning PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) rules regarding large loads co-located at generating facilities 
in the PJM footprint,1 as well as Rule 213 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,2 
Antora Energy LLC (“Antora”) hereby provides comments on the order issued by the 
Commission in the above-captioned docket and PJM’s response thereto.3  Antora urges the 
Commission to find that the existing Tariff is not just and reasonable, and to require a 
replacement rate that allows for the flexible nature of Antora’s thermal storage load to be 
3 Answer of PJM Interconnection (Mar. 24, 2025) (“PJM Answer”). 
2 18 C.F.R. § 385.213. 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 190 FERC   61,115 (2025) (“Co-location Order”). 
2

appropriately and efficiently accounted for in its study processes, procedures, and transmission 
rates.4  The Commission should direct PJM to build from Options 4 and 7 set forth in the PJM 
Answer to create such a rate,5 while not precluding the development of additional rate designs 
and interconnection processes in the future or in other regions, as may be necessary to integrate 
flexible loads such as those of Antora’s thermal energy storage charging.  
Antora is a U.S. manufacturer of thermal batteries, which are domestically built in San 
Jose, California, and developer of thermal storage projects for industrial facilities in the U.S. and 
abroad.  Antora is at the forefront of an industry that holds tremendous potential to lower the cost 
of industrial processes.  Antora can help support American energy dominance by providing a 
market for off-peak, low-cost power during periods of low demand.  But as explained herein, 
appropriate regulation that facilitates interconnection and transmission service capable of 
accounting for the unique low load factor, highly flexible nature of thermal energy storage 
charging loads is required for this industry to thrive and to maximize its benefits while 
minimizing costs for the grid and its customers.  Specifically, the flexible load profile of thermal 
energy storage facilities allows them to contribute to grid reliability while minimizing grid 
capacity costs and infrastructure costs and making greater use of existing generation and 
transmission infrastructure.  The Commission’s Order to Show Cause creates an important 
opportunity for PJM’s regulatory framework to evolve to meet the needs of Antora and other 
similar customers, remedying deficiencies that render the existing tariff unjust and unreasonable.   
5 See PJM Answer at 13-14, 18-19 (outlining Options 4 and 7 to facilitate co-location 
arrangements).  
4 See Co-location Order at P 87 (requesting comments addressing “(1) whether the 
existing tariff remains just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential” and (2) 
“what changes to the Tariff should be implemented as replacement rates.”)   
3

I.​
Background 
Antora’s thermal batteries will provide heat to industrial operations.  Initial deployments 
will focus on industrial process heat up to ~400C, and future deployments will include 
high-temperature processes such as mineral refining, cement, glass, aluminum, and steel.6  The 
technology uses low cost electricity to resistively super-heat carbon blocks that are capable of 
ultra-fast charging and absorption of heat.  The carbon blocks store the energy as heat, at 
temperatures over 2,000◦C, in a compact thermal battery.  The energy is discharged in the form of 
heat at the scale and temperature needed by large industrial operations.  Antora is also 
developing thermal storage products that allow the energy stored as heat to produce electricity, 
thereby serving as electric energy storage devices. 
Like electro-chemical batteries, a significant portion of Antora’s thermal battery value 
comes from flexibility.  The battery is charged during periods of high energy production and low 
demand, thereby helping reduce curtailment of renewable resources and allowing the thermal 
battery to absorb low value/negatively priced electricity.  Because thermal storage can provide 
24/7 heat over a multi-day period by charging only roughly 1/3 of the time, it can fully avoid 
periods of high demand, high-capacity utilization and high electricity pricing.  This allows 
Antora’s industrial and manufacturing clients to gain the benefits of low-cost periods of excess 
generation without requiring the factories themselves to curtail when low cost power is not 
available and during periods of coincident peak transmission system use and demand.  By 
co-locating an Antora thermal battery with a generation resource, Antora can provide factories 
6 CNN has described Antora’s technology and electricity usage. Weir, B., These hot rocks 
can glow brighter than the sun. They could also help spell the end of fossil fuels (Dec. 18, 2023), 
available at 
https://www.cnn.com/2023/12/16/climate/solution-hot-rocks-renewable-energy-battery/index.ht
ml  
4

with onsite power, heat for industrial processes, and energy storage if necessary.  Co-location of 
highly flexible, low load factor thermal energy storage can allow better utilization of 
variable renewable energy resources that might otherwise be curtailed, without causing 
additional co-incident peak demand and without impacting the ability  of that renewable 
energy project to support resource adequacy goals.  Co-location can also minimize or 
eliminate the already low impacts on the transmission system because thermal energy storage can 
be operated to use only energy from a co-located energy source (and only during hours when that 
resource is not needed for capacity). 
Antora is committed to paying its fair share of grid costs.  The pathway a resource takes 
to interconnect to the system, whether via a supply study process that incorporates co-located 
load or through an Electric Distribution Company (“EDC”) or Transmission Owner (“TO”) 
process for interconnecting load alone, should not itself cause disparate rate treatment 
independent of the characteristics of the underlying load and generation facilities.  At the same 
time, however, study processes should account for load shape, flexibility, and dispatchability 
when determining the infrastructure necessary to serve that load.  Companies like Antora should 
not be required to fund infrastructure or secure network resources that they do not need.  Antora 
can follow curtailment instructions from grid operators (including Regional Transmission 
Organizations (RTOs) and EDCs) if doing so facilitates studying Antora’s load in a manner that 
appropriately accounts for its flexibility and low load-factor.

III.​
Motion to Intervene Out of Time 
As the developer of facilities with large and flexible thermal battery loads that may often 
be co-located with generation facilities, Antora’s interests cannot be represented by any other 
party and its intervention is in the public interest.  Antora respectfully requests that the 
Commission grant this request to intervene out-of-time.  Antora accepts the record as it stands, 
and this intervention will not place any additional burden on any other party, nor will it disrupt or 
delay Commission proceedings in this matter. 
IV.​
Comments 
PJM’s existing tariff is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory because it does 
not offer any study process or form of transmission service that properly accounts for highly 
flexible and low load factor loads such as Antora’s thermal energy storage.  This yields higher 
costs or delays for the developers of flexible load facilities and for other customers, delays the 
interconnection of new loads, and fails to use the full capabilities of these loads to enhance 
system reliability.   
The Commission should order PJM to remedy these deficiencies by developing a 
replacement rate that builds from Options 4 and 7 set forth in PJM’s Answer.  Specifically, the 
Commission should direct PJM to enable Option 4 by modifying its interconnection procedures 
to facilitate the study of co-located loads.7  In addition, the Commission should direct PJM to 
build out Option 7 by developing a new non-capacity backed service offering.  However, unlike 
Option 7 in PJM’s filing which suggests only a transitional service product, the Commission 
should direct PJM to provide such service on a permanent or transitional basis, subject to the 
7 As described in Section IV.B.1 below, Antora supports potential modifications to Option 
4 to limit reliability risk and resource adequacy and capacity price risks for other customers, to 
the extent the Commission deems such modifications necessary.  
 
6

election of the transmission customer.  These tariff revisions are not mutually exclusive with the 
development of additional options set forth in the PJM Answer that may be beneficial, such as 
Option 6 to provide a faster path to studying new generation co-located with new load or Option 
8 to facilitate more effective participation of Network Load as demand response.8  The 
Commission could integrate the new flexible service interconnection pathways with any of the 
other options it may direct PJM to pursue, and should make clear that its order remedying PJM’s 
tariff does not preclude the development of additional pathways to interconnect and serve 
co-located load in PJM or elsewhere.  
A.​
PJM’s tariff is unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory in failing to 
appropriately study and incorporate flexible loads 
PJM outlines two sets of potential pathways for co-located load to connect to the system, 
but neither of them appropriately incorporates highly flexible, low load factor flexible loads.   
The first set of potential pathways relies on the generator interconnection procedures, 
with loads connecting behind a generator’s Point of Interconnection using PJM’s necessary study 
8 PJM explains that Option 6 “would also be open for existing generation that could serve 
the energy needs of the large loads so long as the generator would still be available to PJM as a 
Capacity Resource.”  PJM Answer at 16.  Antora facilities could co-locate with existing 
generation in this manner, drawing from the co-located generation only when it is not needed for 
capacity purposes.  To operationalize such a process, PJM could develop a mechanism through 
which it can provide automated curtailment instructions to the load so that the load can avoid 
drawing from the generation whenever the generation is needed for resource adequacy.  
Modifications may be required to PJM’s capacity accreditation to ensure that credit is based on 
the generation’s availability to PJM when needed, rather than on its total energy output to the 
PJM system.  Option 8 is beneficial insofar as it may facilitate more effective demand response 
participation, but it does nothing to remedy the problems in PJM’s study processes that fail to 
account for or leverage the flexibility of load to minimize transmission infrastructure costs and 
rely on fewer Network Resources to serve the same amount of load.   
7

process.9   These pathways offer a significant efficiency advantage over studying load separately 
from the colocated generation, as they assess the electrical impacts of proposed new generation 
and load in a single interconnection process.  As the record in Docket No. AD24-11 makes clear, 
co-location offers a host of potential benefits, including reduced infrastructure costs.10  A single 
study process will better ensure that these savings are accurately captured.  It also reduces project 
risk for the developer where the proposed new energy supply resource and co-located load are 
commercially reliant on one another, as being studied in a single process allows the different 
project components to receive study results on the same timeline, make decisions about 
milestone payments, and demonstrate commercial readiness in a single forum.  But this set of 
pathways fails to provide an adequate pathway for flexible loads because, as PJM explains, it 
“does not have a tariffed study process for load.”11  The Tariff’s study procedures lack the 
necessary detail to inform customers such as Antora how their charging loads will be studied and 
confirm that the loads’ flexibility will be accounted for.  The process has high transaction costs, 
as it requires the development of bespoke agreements.  In a recent proceeding, the Commission 
rejected a non-conforming interconnection agreement providing for a load to be studied under 
this process where the underlying agreement presented generalized co-location issues rather than 
unique concerns particular to the individual customer.12   
12 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC   61,078 (2024), order on reh’g, 191 FERC   
61,025 (2025). 
11 PJM Answer at 47.  The Commission suggests that PJM’s necessary study process is 
not adequate to study the reliability impacts of co-located loads.  See Co-location Order at P 79.  
10 See, e.g., Pre-technical Conference Comments of the Clean Energy Buyers Association, 
Docket No. AD24-11, at 17-19 (Oct. 25, 2024).  
 
9 See PJM Answer at 47-50 (outlining how and when PJM conducts its necessary study 
process for co-located load and explaining that load studied pursuant to this path way may or 
may not register as Network Load).  
8

The second set of pathways requires load to register as Network Load.  But as PJM states, 
its transmission planning, operating protocols, and procedures for providing service to Network 
Load do not account for load shape and flexibility.  Instead, PJM “assumes that it must serve the 
customer’s full load during peak conditions on the system.”13  This assumption is a poor match 
for loads such as Antora’s, which only draw from the system roughly 1/3 of the time and never 
during peak conditions, and are capable of responding immediately to curtailment instructions 
sent by PJM or the relevant EDC.14   
While PJM’s necessary study process to some extent captures the flexibility of co-located 
load, PJM does not capture those benefits where the load is required to register as Network 
Load.15  Per PJM’s response, state law may require a customer to designate load as Network 
15 The Commission directly asked PJM to “explain whether PJM’s necessary study 
process allows a co-location arrangement to demonstrate its capability to flexibly adjust its 
withdrawals from or injections to the transmission system” such as “by curtailing on-site load.”  
Co-location Order at P 88.d.ii.  
 
14 While PJM offers demand response and price responsive demand programs that 
flexible loads may take advantage of in order to capture the value of avoiding electric energy 
consumption during peak demand, these programs do not reflect load flexibility in PJM’s 
transmission planning and operating procedures, which currently do not have a mechanism to 
allow load to respond to transmission system constraints in addition to generation constraints. 
13 PJM Answer at 39 n. 64.  As PJM explains, in “any configuration where the co-located 
load is Network Load” the relevant EDC would conduct “load integration studies . . . in addition 
to necessary studies” performed in PJM’s generation interconnection process.  Id. at 8.  But the 
assumptions that PJM uses for Network Load in its own transmission planning and operations 
are highly relevant for those state-jurisdictional processes, as they define the scope of 
transmission service that will be studied in those processes for non Native Load Customers, and 
Network Service is designed to be comparable to the transmission service that Transmission 
Owners provide to Native Load Customers.  See id. at 39 n. 61 (highlighting the principle of 
comparable service). 
9

Load.16  Further, the necessary study process applies only in the limited circumstance where “the 
load is assumed to never take power from the grid.”17   
Further, as discussed above, PJM’s tariff lacks general language as to how this necessary 
study process will be applied to loads.  PJM notes that “it is possible that the Generation Owner 
could propose a special protection scheme or Remedial Action Scheme (‘RAS’) to reduce the 
load under certain conditions (where, for example, the generating unit comes offline),” but PJM 
does not have any standard language to provide for any such arrangement and appears to 
contemplate load modulation as something that would occur only in an emergency rather than as 
a matter of course, as would occur with Antora’s thermal battery charging.  While PJM’s existing 
Behind the Meter (“BTM”) Generation rules provide one limited pathway to interconnection that 
partially accounts for load flexibility insofar as PJM allows load to be netted with generation 
when calculating Network Load,18 this structure is primarily concerned with rate treatment and 
does not provide for planning, forecasting, and operations procedures that fully leverage the 
flexibility of the underlying load to contribute to grid reliability and use less network 
infrastructure. 
PJM’s failure to offer a service that matches the needs of flexible loads such as those of 
Antora facilities or other co-located facilities with flexible operations capabilities is unjust and 
unreasonable and unduly discriminatory19 because it may delay or prevent the interconnection of 
19 See Calpine Corp. et al. v. PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 163 FERC   61,236, at P 68 n. 
112 (2018) (“Typically, undue discrimination cases involve a seller charging a different rate to 
similarly-situated customers; but undue discrimination can also occur when a seller charges the 
18 Id. at 35. 
17 PJM Answer at 51.  Under this study process, “the generator’s Capacity 
Interconnection Rights” are “reduced by the expected peak MW utilization of the co-located 
load.”  Id. 
16 PJM Answer at 14. 
 
10

these loads,20 trigger the construction of infrastructure that is not needed to serve them, and fail 
to incentivize customers to provide operational flexibility that could benefit the system.  
To the extent PJM requires all loads to register as Network Load and assumes it must 
serve the customer’s full peak load during peak conditions even if the load is flexible and could 
be curtailed at PJM’s direction, this is likely to overcharge both the interconnecting load 
customer, and other customers on the system for transmission service or interconnecting 
facilities.  It overcharges the interconnecting loads because, as PJM explains, “[t]he costs of new 
facilities required to interconnect the new Network Load are charged to the Network 
Customer.”21  Where a customer could have instead taken curtailable transmission service that 
allows PJM and/or the EDC to curtail its load if that service were offered, the failure to provide a 
service option that incorporates load flexibility will directly lead to costs for the interconnecting 
customer that do not appropriately reflect its flexibility and resulting ability to avoid using high 
value energy or grid capacity.22  And it will lead to increased costs for other customers because 
PJM’s transmission and interconnection study processes and operating protocols will apply a 
lack of headroom in its system based on its assumed need to serve the entirety of the Network 
22 Depending on how PJM interprets its Tariff, this requirement may also require a 
flexible load to secure more Network Resources than would be necessary to provide service to 
the load if its flexibility were properly accounted for.  In the context of developing a project in 
another RTO, the RTO has indicated that the LSE serving Antora must secure an amount of 
network resources to match the non-coincident peak load of the proposed Antora facility, a 
requirement that would substantially increase the project’s costs. 
21 PJM Answer at 40. 
20 While interconnection processes for retail customers are generally administered by 
EDCs pursuant to state jurisdictional processes, an EDC taking Network Integration 
Transmission Service from PJM must account for the terms of that service when designing retail 
rates, services, and interconnection processes.  
 
same rate to differently-situated customers.”).  
 
11

Load at any given moment, despite the fact that the customer is capable of dispatching down 
pursuant to PJM and/or EDC instructions.23  This, in turn, will trigger identification of 
infrastructure upgrades that could have been avoided, with such costs either allocated pursuant to 
PJM’s applicable transmission planning process or else attributed to other Network Customers or 
interconnecting supply resources, depending on which study process identifies a need for 
infrastructure based on the assumption that the load may need to be served at any moment even 
though it is flexible and dispatchable. 
By failing to offer a transmission service suited to flexible load, PJM also provides a 
disincentive to load flexibility that will yield higher capacity supply costs.  PJM explains that 
whether or not Network Load is flexible, “PJM will include the customer’s full load in the RPM 
for purposes of procuring adequate capacity to serve the load.”24  As PJM explains, “where 
conditions are tight, any additional load on the system requires either the addition of supply 
resources to serve that load reliably, or flexibility on the part of the load to curtail its 
consumption from the transmission system when necessary to maintain reliability.”25  To the 
extent that rates do not facilitate “supply and operational flexibility,” the system will require 
more resources to provide the same level of reliability in service to customers, rendering rates 
unjust and unreasonable.”26  If properly incorporated into PJM’s operations, fully flexible load 
such as that of Antora’s facilities need not impose any new resource adequacy burden.  Antora 
supports a rate mechanism and operations protocols that would allow PJM to direct Antora to 
26 Co-location Order at P 85. 
25 Id. at 8.  
24 Id. at 39 n. 64.  
23 PJM explains that it “will include the full load in the Load Forecast for purposes of 
PJM’s transmission planning with RTEP.”  PJM Answer at 39 n. 64.  
12

fully curtail its load whenever called upon to do so by PJM and ensure that the Antora load does 
not draw from the system when the grid is stressed either due to insufficient generation supply or 
due to a transmission system constraint. 
The costs of this unnecessary infrastructure and capacity are substantial.  A recent study 
by researchers at the Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability at Duke 
University suggests that nearly 100 GW of additional load could be served using existing 
infrastructure if the load were flexible.27        
B.​
The Commission can order a just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory replacement rate that builds from Options 4 and 7 set forth 
by PJM  
To address the deficiencies that render PJM’s existing tariff unjust, unreasonable, and 
unduly discriminatory, the Commission should direct PJM to revise its tariff so as to enable 
Option 4, and to provide for a non-capacity backed transmission service like that described in 
Option 7 but available on a permanent basis.  These tariff revisions would facilitate the 
integration of highly flexible, low load factor loads co-located with supply resources.  These 
tariff revisions are not mutually exclusive with other tariff mechanisms to support co-location, so 
the Commission should make clear that they do not preclude the development and submission of 
other options set forth in PJM’s filing, or other potential tariff designs not included therein.  
1.​ The Commission should require PJM to revise its tariff so as to facilitate 
interconnection pursuant to PJM’s Option 4 
The Commission should require PJM to enable its proposed Option 4, as this is the only 
27 Tyler Norris et al., Rethinking Load Growth: Assessing the Potential for Integration of 
Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems (2025), available at 
https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/sites/default/files/publications/rethinking-load-growth.pdf.  
While the study focused on headroom to serve peak demand and did not account for certain 
technical constraints of power plants or transmission constraints, it nevertheless suggests very 
significant potential system benefits of integrating flexible load.  Id. at 3, 23. 
13

pathway that allows for the fully coordinated study of co-located generation and load.  As PJM 
explains, tariff modifications are required to implement Option 4 in the wake of the 
Commission’s decision in Docket No. ER24-2172.28  Further, PJM indicates that were it to 
pursue this option, tariff changes would be appropriate to provide for the collection of ancillary 
services charges used by the co-located facilities.29  
While PJM identifies certain aspects of Option 4 that cause PJM to not prefer this option, 
these risks would be mitigated for low-load factor loads such as Antora’s.  Antora would also 
support modifications to this option to ensure that its use does not compromise resource 
adequacy or increase capacity costs for other customers.   
The principal risk cited by PJM with regard to Option 4 is the risk associated with system 
protection facilities needed to prevent delivery of the energy from the grid should the generator 
go offline.”30  This risk is inherently lower for Antora’s thermal battery facilities, as its low load 
30 Id. at 14.  PJM also indicates that it prefers “Network Load” status because it allows for 
“[m]ore comprehensive and holistic system planning based on Network Load status” and 
provides for “[e]nhanced ability to manage load curtailment priority in emergency conditions.”   
Id. at 39.  But as discussed above, PJM’s system planning processes for Network Load do not 
appropriately capture flexible loads.  Antora supports integrating co-located facility loads into 
N-1 operating procedures, but including fully flexible loads in load forecasts and transmission 
plans will overbuild the system.  With regard to load shedding and curtailment, Antora would 
support implementing Option 4 in a manner that ensures the required system protection schemes 
curtail the co-located load in advance the curtailment of other system loads.  PJM also cites a 
potential drawback in not registering co-located load as Network Load of losing “access to 
potential Demand Response capabilities of large co-located loads.”  Id. at 39.  However, 
analogous system benefits could be captured through the design of the relevant protection 
scheme and rules regarding the capacity accreditation of the co-located generation resource.  
FERC should require PJM to design these mechanisms such that the load can be curtailed in 
response to PJM’s direction, thereby leaving the co-located generation available to fully 
contribute to resource adequacy.  
 
29 Id. at 13.  The design of ancillary services charges should reflect the services the 
co-located facility needs.  Inverter-based resources, for example, will require a different mix of 
services than synchronous generating facilities. 
 
28 PJM Answer at 14. 
 
14

factor facilities only charge at times when energy is abundant and low cost.  When the grid is 
stressed, the facilities will not draw from the grid or the co-located generation, allowing the 
co-located generation to support the grid’s needs.  Antora would support limits on the use of 
Option 4, restricting its use only to co-located loads that exhibit these characteristics and thereby 
limiting operational risk.  And while PJM argues that Option 4 “carries operational risk in that 
there is a dependence on the protection system to support reliability,”31 no equipment is immune 
from failure.  PJM can ensure that the use of these protection schemes does not increase overall 
reliability risk to the system by implementing operational standards for such protection schemes, 
and by incorporating them into its N-1 operating protocols.  With these measures in place, a 
failure of system protection equipment would be equivalent to an outage of a generation or 
transmission element on PJM’s system, which the system is designed to reliably overcome. 
Further, while the use of Option 4 potentially raises concerns insofar as it may provide a 
faster pathway to interconnecting new loads to existing generation facilities, thereby impacting 
resource adequacy and capacity costs, these concerns do not apply to Antora’s thermal battery 
loads given their load profile.  Specifically, Antora facilities are designed to draw electric energy 
from the system for charging only when it is abundant and low cost, allowing the co-located 
generation facility to continue to support resource adequacy for the PJM system.  So long as 
accreditation and co-location rules allow for these resources to continue to contribute to system 
resource adequacy, the addition of low-load factor, highly flexible loads such as Antora’s to 
existing facilities will not impact capacity prices or reduce resource adequacy.  Protection 
schemes could ensure not only that co-located loads never draw power from the grid, but also 
could ensure that the loads do not draw energy during times the PJM system requires it for 
31 Id. at 14. 
 
15

resource adequacy, thereby preserving the capacity value of the co-located resource for the 
system.  Antora would support rules that require the use of such protection schemes, and urges 
the Commission to require modification to capacity accreditation rules as necessary to 
appropriately reflect their use.  
2.​ The Commission should require PJM to implement tariff changes that enable 
customers to take non-capacity backed transmission service on a permanent 
basis 
The Commission should also require PJM to develop a new transmission service offering 
like that described in Option 7, but offered on a permanent basis.  PJM’s proposed Option 7 
would provide for “a new non-capacity backed service that could be curtailed in advance of 
emergency procedures.”32  As PJM explains, this service “would allow a large load to integrate 
as Network Load at a potentially faster pace than under existing load integration frameworks.”33  
“[T]he load would avoid capacity costs . . . in return for its willingness to curtail load . . . in those 
situations where, by way of example, PJM has identified conditions that may threaten the 
integrity or reliability of the PJM Region or the regional power system.”34 
PJM suggests offering this service to customers “for a transitional period until any 
resource adequacy supply/demand imbalances associated with the large load addition could be 
addressed and the load could assume full Network Load status with all of its attendant 
benefits.”35  But it also explains that “[p]otential variations on this option could be explored with 
the ultimate goal being to enhance resource adequacy and provide opportunities for large loads to 
35 Id. at 18-19.  
34 Id. at 19.  
33 Id. at 18.  
32 Id. at 9.  
16

efficiently connect to the system by providing incentives for large loads to be more flexible.”36 
Antora urges the Commission to require PJM to offer customers the option of taking this 
service on a permanent rather than transitional basis.  As Antora has explained, its thermal 
storage charging load is inherently flexible.  Unlike high load factor loads which may see 
flexible interconnection as a sub-optimal option that makes sense on a temporary basis in 
exchange for faster interconnection, Antora seeks flexible transmission service throughout the 
life of the facility.  Offering non-capacity backed transmission service on a permanent basis 
would allow PJM to capture the benefits discussed above, serving the same amount of total load 
at lower cost, with less transmission infrastructure and fewer capacity resources.  
​
While PJM’s filing is a significant step forward in indicating a willingness to offer 
non-capacity backed transmission service, it leaves several questions unanswered.  To 
operationalize this proposal, PJM would need to propose detailed tariff provisions describing the 
new type of service and setting forth obligations for the transmission provider and transmission 
customer.  PJM would need to provide a mechanism for PJM and/or the relevant EDC to 
communicate curtailment instructions to the relevant load, providing for operational protocols 
consistent with NERC requirements, as well as a rate structure for the new service.  And it would 
need to provide for operations protocols, including revised N-1 procedures that leverage this 
capability.  PJM should explain how its operations protocols and transmission planning and 
interconnection study assumptions will be adjusted to account for load flexibility and 
dispatchability, as well as describe how it will revise its load forecasting used for determining the 
amount of capacity required to serve customers.  Given that EDCs would continue to administer 
state-jurisdictional processes for load, the Tariff should explain how these processes interact with

Antora notes that in taking such service (either at the PJM level or passed through a

By requiring PJM to build out Option 7 so as to offer permanent transmission service and 
operations protocols that more fully leverage flexible load, the Commission can facilitate the 
integration of more load, more quickly, at lower total cost to customers, while also reducing 
curtailment and thereby supporting the addition of new low-cost variable generation resources.  
V.​
Conclusion 
While the Commission’s inquiry into co-location was initiated in response to a discrete 
challenge involving load locating behind-the-meter of large generating facilities, it has 
spotlighted a broader challenge in serving rapidly growing load with an aging grid and outdated 
interconnection processes for load and generation that too frequently result in unacceptable 
delays.  The Commission’s Co-Location Order takes an important step forward in finding that 
the PJM tariff may be unjust and unreasonable in several respects, and the Commission 
appropriately highlights the potential benefits of flexible facilities.   
To its credit, PJM expresses a willingness to take significant steps forward in evolving its

transmission service and study processes to meet the needs of load and generation in a timelier 
and more affordable way.  But to make rapid progress, the Commission must give PJM clear 
instructions in developing its replacement rate.  By implementing Option 4, PJM can provide for 
an efficient study process and more fully capture the benefits of co-located facilities.  And 
facilitating non-capacity backed transmission service by offering Option 7 on a permanent as 
well as temporary basis is a ‘no regrets’ measure that will help PJM and the nation address the 
building crisis in serving load without precluding the pursuit of other service or options, and 
without inappropriately shifting system costs.
